WHO CAN SIGN FOR A CORPORATION OR LLC: OFFICER SIGNATURES, CORPORATIONS CODE § 313, AND SNUKAL V. FLIGHTWAYS (WITH § 17703.01 FOR LLCS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Widgets, Inc.

SIGNING AUTHORITY AND CORPORATIONS CODE SECTION 313 — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Acme Widgets, Inc. and the question of who can sign an instrument that binds it. It records that Jordan Lee, whose title with Acme Widgets, Inc. is stated here as President, Chief Financial Officer, and Secretary, is the person whose signature is under consideration, and that the instrument in question, if any, is described as: two-year lease of 123 Main Street, signed March 1, 2026. The sheet describes what California statutes and the California Supreme Court say about that question: the officers a California corporation is required to have and the rule that one person may hold several offices (Corporations Code section 312); the rule in Corporations Code section 313 that a written instrument signed by specified officers is not invalidated as to the corporation by the signing officers' lack of authority unless the other party actually knew of it; the Supreme Court's construction of that statute in Snukal v. Flightways Manufacturing, Inc. (2000) — a conclusive rather than rebuttable presumption, an actual-knowledge standard that dispenses with proof of justifiable reliance, a requirement of one officer from each of two categories, and a holding that a single person who in fact holds offices in both categories satisfies the statute even when the instrument lists only one title; the common-law doctrines of express and ostensible authority that remain available when the signer is not one of the specified officers (including Civil Code sections 2317 and 2334); Corporations Code section 208's limits on asserting a corporation's internal restrictions against third parties; and the parallel agency and two-manager signing rules for limited liability companies in Corporations Code section 17703.01. Whether Jordan Lee in fact held any office or position with Acme Widgets, Inc. when any instrument was signed, what Acme Widgets, Inc.'s articles, bylaws, operating agreement, or board resolutions provide, and what the other party to any instrument knew are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming a person, a title, and an instrument here does not itself establish that any rule described below applies, and this sheet states what the statutes and the court say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular contract, dispute, or signature.

THE OFFICERS A CALIFORNIA CORPORATION MUST HAVE, AND THE RULE THAT ONE PERSON MAY HOLD ANY NUMBER OF OFFICES (CORP. CODE § 312)
Corporations Code section 312 sets the minimum slate of officers for a corporation governed by the General Corporation Law. Subdivision (a) provides that a corporation shall have a chairperson of the board (who may be given the title chair of the board, chairperson of the board, or chairperson) or a president, or both; a secretary; a chief financial officer; and such other officers, with such titles and duties as are stated in the bylaws or determined by the board, as may be necessary to enable the corporation to sign instruments and share certificates. The president — or, if there is no president, the chairperson of the board — is the corporation's general manager and chief executive officer unless the articles or bylaws provide otherwise. The same subdivision states that any number of offices may be held by the same person unless the articles or bylaws provide otherwise. Subdivision (b) provides that, except as the articles or bylaws otherwise provide, officers are chosen by the board and serve at the pleasure of the board, subject to any rights an officer has under a contract of employment. The one-person-many-offices rule in subdivision (a) is the statutory premise on which the Supreme Court relied in Snukal v. Flightways Manufacturing, Inc. (2000), discussed in the clauses that follow, when it held that a single individual holding two of the offices named in section 313 can satisfy that section by signing alone.

CORPORATIONS CODE SECTION 313: AN INSTRUMENT SIGNED BY THE SPECIFIED OFFICERS IS NOT INVALIDATED BY THEIR LACK OF AUTHORITY ABSENT THE OTHER PARTY'S ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE
Corporations Code section 313 addresses the enforceability, against the corporation, of a written instrument that its officers signed without authority. Subject to subdivision (a) of section 208 (described in a later clause), the section provides that any note, mortgage, evidence of indebtedness, contract, share certificate, initial transaction statement or written statement, conveyance, or other instrument in writing, and any assignment or endorsement of one, executed or entered into between a corporation and any other person, when signed by the chairperson of the board, the president, or any vice president and the secretary, any assistant secretary, the chief financial officer, or any assistant treasurer of the corporation, is not invalidated as to the corporation by any lack of authority of the signing officers, in the absence of actual knowledge on the part of the other person that the signing officers had no authority to execute it. The Supreme Court in Snukal v. Flightways Manufacturing, Inc. (2000) summarized the section as specifying that an instrument entered into by a corporation is not invalidated by any lack of authority on the part of the officers executing it if (1) it has been executed by the designated officers and (2) the other party does not have actual knowledge that the signing officers lacked authority to execute it. The court also observed that the section was part of the 1975 revision of the Corporations Code, effective January 1, 1977, which repealed the former statute under which a corporate seal on an instrument was prima facie evidence of corporate authority.

WHAT SECTION 313 IS FOR: A "SAFE HARBOR" LETTING THIRD PARTIES RELY ON THE ASSERTIVE AUTHORITY OF SENIOR OFFICERS (SNUKAL)
In Snukal v. Flightways Manufacturing, Inc. (2000), the California Supreme Court explained the purpose behind section 313 before deciding how it applies. The court quoted the Legislative Committee comment to the section, which states that its purpose is to allow third parties to rely upon the assertive authority of various senior executive officers of the corporation concerning the execution of any instrument on behalf of the corporation, and quoted an earlier Court of Appeal decision for the proposition that such extra protection for third parties who deal with corporations is warranted because corporations necessarily act through agents. The court described the section as designed to establish a level of formality that, once attained because the requisite number and type of officers have executed the instrument, affords the third party protection from later efforts by the corporation to disavow its agents' authority in order to avoid its obligations under the agreement. In the court's words, section 313 thus creates a safe harbor for persons entering into an agreement with a corporation: under the section, a corporation may not disclaim its authorization of those persons entering into an agreement on its behalf.

A CONCLUSIVE, NOT REBUTTABLE, PRESUMPTION; AN ACTUAL-KNOWLEDGE STANDARD THAT DISPENSES WITH PROOF OF JUSTIFIABLE RELIANCE; OTHER DEFENSES PRESERVED (SNUKAL)
The Supreme Court in Snukal drew three consequences from the text of section 313. First, if the section's criteria are met, it precludes the invalidation of an instrument entered into by a corporation despite the presentation of evidence demonstrating that the signing officers lacked authority to execute it; the statute therefore provides a conclusive, rather than a merely rebuttable, evidentiary presumption of authority on the part of the specified officers. The court contrasted this with the repealed corporate-seal statute, which had created only a rebuttable presumption. Second, the section applies so long as the other party does not have actual knowledge that the executing officers lack authority. Because it applies even when the other party should have, but does not have, actual knowledge of the officers' lack of authority, that party is relieved of the burden of establishing justifiable reliance upon the officers' authority — a burden the common law of ostensible authority otherwise imposes. As the court put it, the statute limits the burden of proof, insofar as the third party's knowledge is concerned, to a showing that he or she did not have actual knowledge of any lack of authority on the part of the signing officers. Third, in a footnote, the court stressed that when section 313 applies and the corporation is prevented from invalidating the agreement by asserting its signing officers' lack of authority, the corporation is not thereby prevented from asserting the agreement's invalidity on an alternative theory other than lack of authority, such as fraud, mistake, or failure of consideration.

SECTION 313 REQUIRES A SIGNATURE FROM EACH OF TWO CATEGORIES OF OFFICER — ONE "OPERATIONAL," ONE "FINANCIAL" — NOT THE PRESIDENT ALONE (SNUKAL)
Section 313 lists the chairperson of the board, the president, or any vice president "and" the secretary, any assistant secretary, the chief financial officer, or any assistant treasurer. In Snukal the Supreme Court held that the section is ambiguous as to how those lists combine and resolved the ambiguity by reference to the statute's purpose. The court concluded that the Legislature apparently considered that execution of an instrument by two officers — one officer having general, operational responsibilities (the chairman of the board, president, or any vice-president) and one officer having recordkeeping or financial responsibilities (the secretary, assistant secretary, chief financial officer, or treasurer) — sufficed to earn the statute's protection, and it agreed with the commentators who had read the section that way. The court rejected the plaintiff's alternative reading under which the chairman of the board or the president signing alone would bring an instrument within the section, reasoning that this would create a safe harbor coextensive with every instrument executed by, for example, the corporation's president, when the statute's function is to absolve the third party of the common-law burden of proving that the president had actual or ostensible authority. The court accordingly construed the section to apply only when at least two officers — one from each of the two series or categories designated — execute the instrument, and summarized its conclusion as applying section 313 only when a given instrument has been executed by one officer in the first, operational category and one in the second, financial category.

ONE PERSON WHO ACTUALLY HOLDS AN OFFICE IN EACH CATEGORY SATISFIES SECTION 313 BY SIGNING ALONE, EVEN IF THE INSTRUMENT LISTS ONLY ONE TITLE (SNUKAL)
The facts of Snukal presented the two-category requirement in its most common small-business form. Kirt Lyle was the president, chief financial officer, and secretary of Flightways Manufacturing, Inc. On the corporation's behalf, Lyle alone executed a two-year residential lease, designating his title as president without indicating that he also was chief financial officer and secretary. When the corporation fell behind on rent and was sued, it denied that Lyle had been authorized to enter into the lease, and the Court of Appeal held that section 313 did not apply because only one officer had signed. The Supreme Court reversed. Reading section 313 together with section 312 — which requires at minimum a chairman of the board or a president, a secretary, and a chief financial officer, but permits the same individual to hold multiple offices — the court observed that section 313 contains no language directing that the signing officers be separate individuals or that they specify the office or offices they hold. It therefore held that although section 313 applies only where officers in each of the two designated categories execute the instrument, the section is satisfied when one individual who in fact holds two of the specified offices executes it. The court added that the Legislature did not intend to limit the statute to instances in which two corporate offices are set forth on the face of the instrument; rather, the signature of one person alone is sufficient to bind a corporation as long as he or she holds corporate offices in each of the two categories the statute describes. Because Lyle served both as Flightways's president and as its chief financial officer (and secretary), and because the landlord did not have actual knowledge of any lack of authority on Lyle's part, the lease was not invalidated by Lyle's lack of authority to enter into it on the corporation's behalf.

WHEN THE SIGNER IS NOT ONE OF THE SPECIFIED OFFICERS: EXPRESS AND OSTENSIBLE AUTHORITY AT COMMON LAW, AND THE HEAVIER BURDEN OF PROOF (SNUKAL; CIV. CODE §§ 2317, 2334)
Section 313 does not displace the ordinary law of agency; it adds a statutory shortcut on top of it. The Supreme Court in Snukal stated that the section leaves intact the other party's ability to assert the validity of an instrument under existing common-law doctrines when the signatory or signatories do not hold the corporate offices the statute specifies, quoting the Assembly committee comment that the section does not create any negative inference that a document executed by others than the specified officers without actual authority is invalid, and that the concepts of apparent authority, inherent agency power, and other validating concepts remain effective where applicable. The court summarized the common-law rules as follows. A corporate officer may have express authority to enter into an agreement on behalf of the corporation, granted by the board of directors or the corporate bylaws. Alternatively, an officer may have ostensible authority if he or she assumed and exercised the power in the past with the apparent consent and acquiescence of the corporation; ostensible authority requires justifiable reliance by the third party. At common law the party seeking to enforce a contract with a corporation generally bears the burden of establishing the contracting officer's authority to bind it. When an agreement is not signed by the specified officers, the third party may therefore still seek its validation by invoking traditional common-law theories, but incurs an increased burden of proof. The Civil Code states the general agency rules the court applied: ostensible authority is such as a principal, intentionally or by want of ordinary care, causes or allows a third person to believe the agent to possess (section 2317), and a principal is bound by acts of its agent under a merely ostensible authority only to those persons who have in good faith, and without want of ordinary care, incurred a liability or parted with value upon the faith of it (section 2334).

First, if the section's criteria are met, it precludes the invalidation of an instrument entered into by a corporation despite the presentation of evidence demonstrating that the signing officers lacked authority to execute it; the statute therefore provides a conclusive, rather than a merely rebuttable, evidentiary presumption of authority on the part of the specified officers. Second, the section applies so long as the other party does not have actual knowledge that the executing officers lack authority. As the court put it, the statute limits the burden of proof, insofar as the third party's knowledge is concerned, to a showing that he or she did not have actual knowledge of any lack of authority on the part of the signing officers. Third, in a footnote, the court stressed that when section 313 applies and the corporation is prevented from invalidating the agreement by asserting its signing officers' lack of authority, the corporation is not thereby prevented from asserting the agreement's invalidity on an alternative theory other than lack of authority, such as fraud, mistake, or failure of consideration.

expectedJSON.body: Section 313 lists the chairperson of the board, the president, or any vice president "and" the secretary, any assistant secretary, the chief financial officer, or any assistant treasurer. In Snukal the Supreme Court held that the section is ambiguous as to how those lists combine and resolved the ambiguity by reference to the statute's purpose. The court concluded that the Legislature apparently considered that execution of an instrument by two officers — one officer having general, operational responsibilities (the chairman of the board, president, or any vice-president) and one officer having recordkeeping or financial responsibilities (the secretary, assistant secretary, chief financial officer, or treasurer) — sufficed to earn the statute's protection, and it agreed with the commentators who had read the section that way. The court rejected the plaintiff's alternative reading under which the chairman of the board or the president signing alone would bring an instrument within the section, reasoning that this would create a safe harbor coextensive with every instrument executed by, for example, the corporation's president, when the statute's function is to absolve the third party of the common-law burden of proving that the president had actual or ostensible authority. The court accordingly construed the section to apply only when at least two officers — one from each of the two series or categories designated — execute the instrument, and summarized its conclusion as applying section 313 only when a given instrument has been executed by one officer in the first, operational category and one in the second, financial category.

expectedJSON.body: The facts of Snukal presented the two-category requirement in its most common small-business form. Kirt Lyle was the president, chief financial officer, and secretary of Flightways Manufacturing, Inc. On the corporation's behalf, Lyle alone executed a two-year residential lease, designating his title as president without indicating that he also was chief financial officer and secretary. When the corporation fell behind on rent and was sued, it denied that Lyle had been authorized to enter into the lease, and the Court of Appeal held that section 313 did not apply because only one officer had signed. The Supreme Court reversed. Reading section 313 together with section 312 — which requires at minimum a chairman of the board or a president, a secretary, and a chief financial officer, but permits the same individual to hold multiple offices — the court observed that section 313 contains no language directing that the signing officers be separate individuals or that they specify the office or offices they hold. It therefore held that although section 313 applies only where officers in each of the two designated categories execute the instrument, the section is satisfied when one individual who in fact holds two of the specified offices executes it. The court added that the Legislature did not intend to limit the statute to instances in which two corporate offices are set forth on the face of the instrument; rather, the signature of one person alone is sufficient to bind a corporation as long as he or she holds corporate offices in each of the two categories the statute describes. Because Lyle served both as Flightways's president and as its chief financial officer (and secretary), and because the landlord did not have actual knowledge of any lack of authority on Lyle's part, the lease was not invalidated by Lyle's lack of authority to enter into it on the corporation's behalf.

On behalf of Flightways, Lyle alone executed the lease agreement, designating his title as president, without indicating that he also was chief financial officer and secretary of the corporation.

citations.quote: Thus, Corporations Code section 312 requires that a corporation designate, at minimum, a chairman of the board or a president, plus a secretary and a treasurer. At the same time, that statute permits the same individual to hold multiple corporate offices. Corporations Code section 313 does not contain any language directing that the signing officers be separate individuals, or that the signing officers specify the office or offices they hold. Accordingly, although Corporations Code section 313 applies only where corporate officers in each of the two designated series or categories execute the instrument, that statute, considered in light of Corporations Code section 312, is satisfied when one individual who in fact holds two of the specified corporate offices executes the instrument.

expectedJSON.body: Section 313 does not displace the ordinary law of agency; it adds a statutory shortcut on top of it. The Supreme Court in Snukal stated that the section leaves intact the other party's ability to assert the validity of an instrument under existing common-law doctrines when the signatory or signatories do not hold the corporate offices the statute specifies, quoting the Assembly committee comment that the section does not create any negative inference that a document executed by others than the specified officers without actual authority is invalid, and that the concepts of apparent authority, inherent agency power, and other validating concepts remain effective where applicable. The court summarized the common-law rules as follows. A corporate officer may have express authority to enter into an agreement on behalf of the corporation, granted by the board of directors or the corporate bylaws. Alternatively, an officer may have ostensible authority if he or she assumed and exercised the power in the past with the apparent consent and acquiescence of the corporation; ostensible authority requires justifiable reliance by the third party. At common law the party seeking to enforce a contract with a corporation generally bears the burden of establishing the contracting officer's authority to bind it. When an agreement is not signed by the specified officers, the third party may therefore still seek its validation by invoking traditional common-law theories, but incurs an increased burden of proof. The Civil Code states the general agency rules the court applied: ostensible authority is such as a principal, intentionally or by want of ordinary care, causes or allows a third person to believe the agent to possess (section 2317), and a principal is bound by acts of its agent under a merely ostensible authority only to those persons who have in good faith, and without want of ordinary care, incurred a liability or parted with value upon the faith of it (section 2334).

The comment of the Assembly committee advises that Corporations Code section 313 “does not create any negative inference that a document executed by others than the specified officers without actual authority is invalid; the concepts of the apparent authority and inherent agency power and other validating concepts, where applicable, remain effective to prevent a defense against enforcement of a contract on grounds of lack of authority.”

expectedJSON.body: Section 313 opens with the words "Subject to the provisions of subdivision (a) of Section 208," and section 208 supplies the broader rule against which section 313 operates. Subdivision (a) provides that no limitation upon the business, purposes, or powers of the corporation, or upon the powers of the shareholders, officers, or directors, or the manner of exercising those powers, contained in or implied by the articles, by Chapters 18, 19, and 20 of the General Corporation Law, or by any shareholders' agreement, shall be asserted as between the corporation or any shareholder and any third person — except in three kinds of proceedings: (1) a proceeding by a shareholder or the state to enjoin the doing or continuation of unauthorized business by the corporation or its officers, where third parties have not acquired rights; (2) a proceeding to dissolve the corporation; or (3) a proceeding by the corporation, or by a shareholder suing in a representative suit, against the officers or directors for violation of their authority. Subdivision (b) provides that any contract or conveyance made in the name of a corporation which is authorized or ratified by the board, or is done within the scope of the authority, actual or apparent, conferred by the board or within the agency power of the officer executing it (except as the board's authority is limited by law other than the General Corporation Law), binds the corporation, and the corporation acquires rights under it, whether the contract is executed or wholly or in part executory. Subdivision (c) extends the section to contracts and conveyances made by foreign corporations in California and to all conveyances by foreign corporations of California real property.

Chapters 18, 19, and 20 of the General Corporation Law, cross-referenced in subdivision (a), govern dissolution and related proceedings and are not quoted here. The Snukal opinion mentions section 208(a) only to say, in a footnote, that it "does not differentiate among the types of officers whose exercise of power might be challenged in such a proceeding and therefore does not assist" the interpretation of section 313; the opinion does not construe section 208(b), and no decision construing the interaction of sections 208(b) and 313 was fetched for this sheet. The relationship described in the clause's first sentence — that section 208 supplies the broader rule against which section 313 operates — is this sheet's own characterization drawn from the statutory cross-reference, not a quotation. The subdivision (b) phrase "except as the board’s authority is limited by law other than this division" is reproduced in the quotation; the body paraphrases "this division" as the General Corporation Law, which is Division 1 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code.

expectedJSON.body: The Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act contains its own answer to who can bind a limited liability company, and it turns on whether the articles of organization say the company is manager-managed. Under section 17703.01(a), unless the articles indicate that the LLC is manager-managed, every member is an agent of the company for the purpose of its business or affairs, and the act of any member — including executing an instrument in the company's name — for the apparent purpose of carrying on the company's business or affairs in the usual way binds the company in the particular matter, unless the member in fact has no authority to act in that matter and the person with whom the member is dealing has actual knowledge of that fact. Under subdivision (b), if the articles indicate that the LLC is manager-managed, no member acting solely as a member is an agent of the company or can bind it or execute any instrument on its behalf, while every manager is an agent whose acts for apparently carrying on the company's business in the usual way bind the company, again unless the manager in fact lacks authority and the other party actually knows it. Subdivision (c) provides that no act of a manager or member in contravention of a restriction on authority binds the company to persons having actual knowledge of the restriction. Subdivision (d) then states an LLC analogue of Corporations Code section 313: notwithstanding subdivision (c), any note, mortgage, evidence of indebtedness, contract, certificate, statement, conveyance, or other instrument in writing, and any assignment or endorsement of one, executed or entered into between an LLC and any other person, when signed by at least two managers — or by one manager, if the articles state that the company is managed by only one manager — is not invalidated as to the company by any lack of authority of the signing managers or manager, in the absence of actual knowledge on the part of the other person that they had no authority to execute it.
